# Mario Peng Lee

> cofounder of condense.chat. making powerful AI accessible to everyone, and safe when it gets there.

I'm cofounder and chief scientist at [condense.chat](https://condense.chat/), which compresses what coding agents send to the model so heavy AI workloads cost less (up to about 70% off long sessions, with basically the same output). I'm also CEO of [Pocketful](https://pocketful.ai/), which brings WhatsApp AI agents to restaurant owners in Argentina. Both are basically the same bet, that AI should be cheap and usable enough for everyone.

My background is in linguistics, computer science and psychology (UCLA, Phi Beta Kappa). Mostly I'm interested in how minds (human and machine) represent things, and my view is that understanding that is how AI gets cheaper and safer. These days that means open-source interpretability research at [EleutherAI](https://www.eleuther.ai/) through SOAR 2026 (its Summer of Open AI Research, about 2% of applicants accepted), lately on how stable sparse autoencoder features are across seeds.

Before condense I was a senior AI engineer at [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai/), where I built the agent layer, the memory model behind nexos.heartbeat, and a sandboxed code interpreter.

## writing
- [Sparse autoencoder seeds share more than matching shows](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/orphan-latents.md) (2026-10-31): Two sparse autoencoders that differ only in seed match about half their latents one-to-one. A transplant test calibrated on toy worlds estimates the real shared share at 75 to 86%.
- [Same seed, different SAE: GPU noise and seed dependence](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/same-init-different-dictionary.md) (2026-10-31): Rerun a sparse autoencoder with the same seed and data, changing only GPU kernel nondeterminism, and it leaves 43 to 85% as many latents unmatched as a new seed, mostly the same ones.
- [Where role collapse happens in diffusion models](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/role-collapse.md) (2026-10-23): Prompt SDXL for a mouse chasing a cat and you usually get a cat chasing a mouse. My first suspect was CLIP reading prompts as a bag of words, but after ruling out the encoder, guidance, and cross-attention, the problem seems to sit in the UNet itself.
- [Kids vs LLMs at telling a story](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/kids-vs-llm-stories.md) (2026-10-18): Give a five year old and a language model the same wordless picture book. In 2024 the kids kept track of the characters far better than GPT-4. Two years of models later, the best ones tell the story just like the kids do.
- [cyclediffusion: can a picture be a bottleneck?](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cyclediffusion.md) (2026-10-17): I trained a diffusion model so a captioner could read its pictures back into the original sentence. Instead of inventing a secret visual code, it collapsed into texture, and the reason is the reader you train against.
- [A transformer that passes the wug test](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/phonetic5.md) (2026-10-16): I fine-tuned T5 to turn spelling into IPA. Nobody told it English phonology rules, but it says "wugs" with a /z/ and "wuks" with an /s/, just like a kid does.
- [Why linguists keep writing about John and Mary](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/diverse-names.md) (2026-10-15): In linguistics papers, 30% of male names are John and 31% of female names are Mary. A good list of names doesn't fix that, because people still pick from it. A random generator does.
- [Do sparse autoencoders capture manifolds?](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cross-seed-saes.md) (2026-07-15): A concept like "year" lives on a curved manifold, and a single sparse autoencoder often shatters it instead of capturing it whole. Training several SAEs that differ only in random seed and pooling them tiles the manifold back together, right where one SAE dilutes it.
- [block-GRPO: doing RL on a diffusion language model](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/block-grpo.md) (2026-05-09): GRPO needs a log-probability that diffusion LLMs can't give you cheaply. Using the model's own block-autoregressive structure makes most of it exact, and it beat vanilla GRPO by about 10x on tail reward.
- [Infinite context agents, at WIP London](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/infinite-context-agents-wip-london.md) (2026-04-18): At WIP, an Index Ventures x Anthropic event for London AI builders, I presented memgit, git-backed memory that lets agents keep context across sessions instead of starting from zero.
- [Building nexos.heartbeat: the infinite context problem](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/heartbeat.md) (2026-03-01): An always-on AI twin doesn't have a context window problem, it has an infinite context problem. Information theory, the design space, and why our memory is a git repository.
- [Code interpreter: how we built it ourselves](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/code-interpreter-nexos.md) (2026-01-30): How the nexos.ai code interpreter lets a model run real code instead of guessing: what it is for, and the isolated, ephemeral micro-VM sandbox behind it.
- [RAG isn't dead, plain RAG is](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/rethinking-rag.md) (2025-12-04): Why plain RAG breaks on real enterprise knowledge, and what organizing that knowledge first (late chunking, topic clusters, models that navigate a knowledge tree) changes. With Povilas Nagrockas.
- [Context engineering: where AI stops guessing](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/context-engineering.md) (2025-11-19): The hard part of enterprise AI isn't a bigger model, it's getting the right documents, rules and situational awareness in front of the model before it answers.
- [Psychology-inspired agentic AI](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/psychology-inspired-agentic-ai.md) (2025-11-17): Why agents inherit human failure modes, and how psychology and cognitive science (working memory, theory of mind, team size, bias) shape agent design. My write-up of the Tesonet talk.
- [Psychology for agent design, at Tesonet's AI conference](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/psychology-for-agent-design-tesonet.md) (2025-11-14): At Tesonet's AI-Focused Conference in Vilnius I argued that a lot of agent failures are old psychology problems, and that organizing agents like a small team with clear roles helps.
- [GPT-2, IOI, and the sphex problem](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/gpt2-ioi.md) (2025-05-21): A wasp can look like it understands what it's doing right up until you move one thing. I poked at GPT-2's indirect-object circuit the same way, to see whether it understood the task or just had a routine that usually works.
- [Does parameter sharing help? a multitask recommender experiment](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/multitask-training.md) (2025-05-10): I built the same recommender four times to find out whether sharing parameters across tasks helps. It turned out the loss weighting mattered more than the sharing, which is a known and slightly annoying axis.
- [Starting a blog](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/hello.md) (2025-05-01): Why this page exists, and what to expect.

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/orphan-latents.md -->
---
title: Sparse autoencoder seeds share more than matching shows
date: 2026-10-31
summary: Two sparse autoencoders that differ only in seed match about half their latents one-to-one. A transplant test calibrated on toy worlds estimates the real shared share at 75 to 86%.
---

Train two sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the same Llama-3.1-8B activations,
change nothing but the seed, and match their latents one-to-one. About half
come out with no partner. People call these orphans
([Paulo and Belrose](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615) get 30% shared at 131k
latents), and if seeds really learned different features, "the feature for X"
would depend on which seed you happened to train.

In my SOAR 2026 project (EleutherAI's Summer of Open AI Research, supervised
by Gonçalo Paulo), I find that much of the gap comes from how latents are
matched, not from what they learned. If a latent counts as shared when the
other seed's latents can stand in for it, the estimated shared share goes
from about half to **75 to 86%**.

The reason, at least in part, is tiling.
[Bhalla et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119) show that a single
SAE often splits a curved concept (a manifold) into latents that each cover
one patch, which I'll call tiles. Following up my
[earlier toy post](#/blog/cross-seed-saes), the seeds seem to cut the same
thing differently rather than see different things.

Both views below come from trained SAEs. The sphere is a toy: one planted
sphere, two TopK SAEs of width 32 (each input uses only its k strongest
latents), and every point colored by the latent that fires hardest there.
Seed A cuts it into 9 tiles, seed B into 6, and exactly one tile is matched
across seeds, yet both reconstruct the sphere. The temperature view is Llama
layer 28. I sweep "It is v degrees outside" from −30 to 60°C and plot each
seed's tile-only reconstruction on its top three principal components. Seed A
uses 6 tiles and seed B 4, none is matched one-to-one, and after an
orthogonal rotation the two curves line up with $R^2 = .85$ (shuffled
temperatures give below −.5).

[[demo:seed-tiling]]

## why matching misses it

The standard rule solves a Hungarian assignment (the best one-to-one pairing
between two dictionaries) over encoder and decoder directions, and calls a
pair matched if both cosines reach .7. That works for latents that each mean
one thing. But if tile boundaries depend on the seed, no tile of A has to
line up with any tile of B.

The toy worlds (synthetic activations built from planted manifolds) show how
much this matters: 61 to 84% of live latents are orphans, although both seeds
represent every manifold. Wider SAEs make it worse. One sphere goes from 4
tiles to 25, about 99% unmatched, while the seeds' outputs agree at
$R^2 \geq .98$.

## the test

Neither step uses weight similarity. First, I pool both seeds' orphans and
group them by co-firing, using the Ochiai coefficient over their active token
sets:

$$
O_{ij} = \frac{|A_i \cap A_j|}{\sqrt{|A_i|\,|A_j|}}
$$

A 10-nearest-neighbor graph and Leiden community detection split them into
groups, kept only if denser than in degree-preserving shuffles. The recipe
was picked on toy worlds under a rule fixed in advance (so the risk is that
it's tuned to the toy).

Second, I transplant. For each group I remove the host seed's orphans and
insert the donor's, on the same held-out tokens. With $\Delta\mathrm{SSE}(x)$
the rise in the host's reconstruction error when its group is replaced by $x$:

$$
\mathrm{repair} = 1 - \frac{\Delta\mathrm{SSE}(\text{donor})}{\Delta\mathrm{SSE}(\text{empty slot})}
$$

A repair of 1 means the donor fully stands in, and 0 means it's no better
than an empty slot. A group counts as shared if its repair clears a bar
$b = .19$, the lowest bar at which every control donor (firing-matched
latents, a different group, random latents) passes for at most 1% of orphans
in all 16 toy worlds and all 3 real sites. In the toy, every orphan should
have a stand-in, and 86% pass, which is the test's sensitivity $s$. Grouping
and sensitivity were fixed on the toy, and the bar only looks at control
donors, never at the real groups' own repairs.

## what the real models say

The sites are Llama layer 16 MLP, Llama layer 28 residual and Pythia-160m
layer 6 MLP. At $b = .19$, 51 to 65% of grouped orphans transplant, and no
control passes for more than 0.9%. With $m$ the matched share and $T(b)$ the
share of all orphans in transplanting groups:

$$
\mathrm{shared} = m + (1 - m)\,\frac{T(b)}{s}
$$

That moves the matched 51 / 53 / 42% to **75 / 86 / 82% shared** (about
72 / 81 / 76% before dividing by $s$). Dividing by $s$ assumes real
sensitivity matches the toy's, which is the weakest step, so I'd read these
as rough estimates.

Temperature is the cleanest case. 9 of 10 tiles share a blind group with a
tile of the other seed ($p < .001$), and the donor's tiles repair the host
much better than its below-cutoff Hungarian partners do (KL repair uses
Llama's next-token KL instead of SSE):

| donor | SSE repair (host A / B) | KL repair (host A / B) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| same-concept tiles | +.34 / +.35 | +.63 / +.67 |
| Hungarian partners | +.07 / +.23 | +.30 / +.21 |
| firing-matched | −.32 / −.51 | −.20 / −.12 |

## what it doesn't show

Real orphans transplant partly. Repairs form a broad peak around +.2 to +.4
(3 to 6% above .8, against 49% in the toy), so "shared" means much of the
same structure, not a near-copy. Clean tilings like temperature are also rare
(under 0.1% of orphans), so in real models tiling is shown for a few
concepts, not as the general story. Outside those, groups don't transplant
more often than the orphans' Hungarian partners (partners .62 to .63, groups
.51 to .65), and partner cosine barely predicts which orphans transplant
(AUC .52 to .58), so lowering the cutoff doesn't help.

That leaves 14 to 25% unexplained. Some of it is probably real seed variance,
and how much of that needs a different initialization at all is the subject
of the [companion post](#/blog/same-init-different-dictionary). I'd also love
to see whether a learned adapter makes partial transplants full.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/same-init-different-dictionary.md -->
---
title: Same seed, different SAE: GPU noise and seed dependence
date: 2026-10-31
summary: Rerun a sparse autoencoder with the same seed and data, changing only GPU kernel nondeterminism, and it leaves 43 to 85% as many latents unmatched as a new seed, mostly the same ones.
---

Train a sparse autoencoder (SAE) twice with the same seed and the same data,
so the only difference is GPU kernel nondeterminism (for example the order of
atomic adds in the backward pass, which changes rounding). Match the two
dictionaries latent by latent, and you get **.43 to .85 times as many
unmatched latents** as two different seeds give.

It gets stranger with fully deterministic training. Flipping the last bit of
one encoder weight at step 0 leaves half as many unmatched as a new seed on
GPT-2.

This was a side project I ran on my own, out of curiosity, and it bears on
the [orphan latents](#/blog/orphan-latents) from my SOAR project. Much of
what gets called seed dependence doesn't need a different initialization, so
fixing the seed buys less reproducibility than you'd think.

The protocol follows [Summers and Dinneen (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.04514),
who asked the same question for supervised networks. I match latents with
Hungarian assignments over encoder and decoder directions (both cosines
$\geq .7$) and count unmatched live latents. With $u$ the unmatched share
between two seeds and $t$ the share between two runs that differ only in
kernel noise, the noise share is

$$
R_N = \frac{t}{u}
$$

which is a ratio of unmatched shares, not a variance decomposition. Across
TopK SAEs on Pythia-160m and Llama-3.1-8B (bf16 autocast) and GPT-2 Small
(full fp32), it lands between .43 and .85. On GPT-2 it's higher at twice the
learning rate, at equal reconstruction (.57 vs .77), and with a longer budget
(.77 to .85 from 1B to 4B tokens).

[[demo:noise-share]]

## same latents, not just same amount

On its own, a ratio would be consistent with noise breaking some unrelated
set of latents. So I cross-tabulate "unmatched by the perturbation" against
"unmatched by a new seed" and compute a Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio within
firing-frequency deciles, with a threshold of 3 fixed before any result was
read.

Every perturbation clears it: the last-bit flip, kernel noise, and as a
looser check, document order, minibatch composition and a mid-run kernel
switch. Odds ratios run from 4.7 to 28 across two matching rules. On Llama, a
noise twin (a run that differs only in kernel noise) leaves unmatched 56% of
the latents a new seed leaves unmatched, against 37% expected by chance.

## the first ten steps

In full-fp32 GPT-2, about 122k steps long, the outcome is basically decided
in the first 10 steps. If I train deterministically up to a fork point and
only then let kernel noise in, every one of nine forks from step 10 onward
ends as the same SAE (all latents matched).

Resetting Adam's moments at 1% of training partly reopens the sensitivity.
That seems to me consistent with the optimizer state damping late noise,
though I haven't pinned a mechanism. It isn't universal either: on Pythia at
4k latents the window is still open at 5%, while GPT-2 under bf16 autocast
closes by 1%, so it's probably not the precision (width, model and training
loop all differ).

## where the two SAEs differ

The unmatched latents are also where the two SAEs really differ. After
permutation alignment, the largest rise in held-out FVU (fraction of variance
unexplained) on the straight line between two seeds is 16 to 22% of the
endpoints' value, against 7% for noise twins, and it disappears when only the
matched latents are interpolated. This is the linear mode connectivity test
from [Frankle et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05671).

A couple of caveats. $R_N$ inherits the .7 cosine cutoff, so it measures how
often matching breaks, not how far apart the dictionaries are (the transplant
test in the companion post suggests the functional gap is smaller). And
Pythia and Llama have one seed pair and one twin pair each, so their ratios
don't include pair-to-pair spread. I'd read the range as rough.

The natural next step is to join the two projects: are the latents kernel
noise breaks the orphans that transplant, or the 14 to 25% that don't? I'd
also be curious whether a recipe that damps those first few steps buys more
reproducibility than seed averaging does.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/role-collapse.md -->
---
title: Where role collapse happens in diffusion models
date: 2026-10-23
summary: Prompt SDXL for a mouse chasing a cat and you usually get a cat chasing a mouse. My first suspect was CLIP reading prompts as a bag of words, but after ruling out the encoder, guidance, and cross-attention, the problem seems to sit in the UNet itself.
---

If you prompt SDXL with "a mouse chasing a cat", about three times in four you
get a cat chasing a mouse. The same goes for "a horse riding an astronaut" or
"a doll holding a grandpa": both entities show up, in the roles they usually
have. [Malakouti and Kovashka](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10037) call this role
collapse. I wanted to know which part of the pipeline is responsible, so I went
through the obvious suspects one at a time. My answer so far is that the text
encoder isn't the problem: the denoiser seems to get the roles and draws the
usual pairing anyway.

The prompts follow their RoleBench setup: 10 relations, each in a common
direction and a rare reversed one, active and passive voice, 4 images per
prompt. A vision-language judge labeled each image correct, reversed, or
neither. On a few hundred images I labeled myself, it sometimes calls a
direction where I'd say neither (so the reversed rates are probably a bit
high), but when it picks a direction it agrees with me.

## suspect one: CLIP

This was my first guess. CLIP is known to treat captions a lot like a bag of
words ([Yuksekgonul et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01936)), and it
reads left to right, so in "a photo of one cat chasing one mouse" the cat token
is computed before the verb exists. A linear probe for the role of the first
noun sits at chance (0.50) in both of SDXL's CLIP encoders, so SDXL really is
getting role-blind noun tokens.

T5-XXL is the opposite. The first noun's role is decodable at about 1.00,
including on relations the probe never saw, and in later layers the probe also
works on sentences like "one mouse that one cat is chasing", which have no
"being" in them. My read is that T5 encodes the actual role, not just word order.

SD3.5-Large uses T5 alongside CLIP, which makes it a clean test. If CLIP were
the cause, SD3.5 should do better. It doesn't:

```
rare prompts, reversed rate
SDXL                       0.74
SD3.5-Large                0.72-0.75
SD3.5, T5 only             0.45-0.57
```

Zeroing the CLIP inputs lowers the reversed rate, but almost all of that moves
to "neither" (a missing lion, a baby held instead of fed), and correct only
goes up by about 4 points. When both entities are drawn, they still have the
usual roles.

## suspect two: weak conditioning

Maybe the model has the roles but the prior outweighs them, and stronger
guidance would push them through. On SDXL, CFG 3, 7, and 12 all leave rare
prompts 68-74% reversed, and so does passive voice (78%) and IterComp, a
fine-tune trained for composition (76%). The pictures do change between
settings, just not who is doing what.

[[demo:role-collapse-rates]]

## suspect three: cross-attention

Another option is that the noun tokens leak into each other's image regions.
They don't seem to. In reversed images the attention maps for the two nouns
are as separate as in correct ones (top-10% IoU 0.054 vs 0.053). Each noun gets
its own region, and the model draws that entity in its usual pose.

## suspect four: some part of the conditioning

Last, I tried splicing on SDXL: replace the verb, EOS, or pooled embedding with
the one from the role-swapped prompt and see whether the drawn roles follow.
None of these moved the reversed rate by more than about 4 points, which is
within noise. My guess at why comes from comparing the two prompts with no
splicing at all:

```
P(drawn as "A verbs B"), prompt "A verbs B" vs "B verbs A"
common pairs     0.76 vs 0.74
other pairs      0.48 vs 0.45
```

Swapping the whole sentence changes the result by about 3 points. Most of the
outcome is set by which two nouns are in the prompt, so there isn't much role
signal for a splice to find.

## what's left

That leaves the denoiser itself (the UNet in SDXL, the MMDiT in SD3.5). With
T5 the roles are in the text embedding, and SD3.5 draws what's typical for the
noun pair anyway.

If the failure really is inside the UNet, then a
model that does draw reversed roles, like the LoRA from the ReBind paper, should
differ from base SDXL somewhere in there. My plan is to train a
[block-sparse featurizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25234) (BSF, a sparse
autoencoder whose features are small subspaces) on UNet activations from both
models, and look for a block that tracks the reversal. The part I'm most
curious about is whether that block is separate from the ones for the subject
and object. If it is, role would be its own feature in the UNet, something you
could probably steer directly.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/kids-vs-llm-stories.md -->
---
title: Kids vs LLMs at telling a story
date: 2026-10-18
summary: Give a five year old and a language model the same wordless picture book. In 2024 the kids kept track of the characters far better than GPT-4. Two years of models later, the best ones tell the story just like the kids do.
---

Hand a five year old a wordless picture book and they'll tell you a story:
"a dog finds a paint can, and then he knocks it over, and then he sees a
cat..." The dog stays the dog the whole way through. In 2024, GPT-4 doing
the same task lost track of its characters much more often than the kids
did. Two years of models later, the best ones are basically
indistinguishable from them, at least on this measure.

## the setup

With Amalia Ionescu and Catherine Sandhofer at UCLA's Language and Cognitive
Development Lab, we had 31 children aged 4 to 6 narrate *Bow Meow Wow* by
Priya Kuriyan (Pratham Books, CC BY 4.0), a wordless book where a dog tips
over a paint can, meets a cat, and the two end up making a painting. They
went page by page. The models got the same pages, one image per turn, and
told stories of about the same length (115 to 200 words
vs the kids' 154).

To measure how well each storyteller keeps track of characters we used
coreference resolution ([FastCoref](https://github.com/shon-otmazgin/fastcoref)),
which groups every mention of the same entity ("a dog ... he ... the yellow
dog") into a chain. The longer the chains, the more the story keeps coming
back to the same characters instead of losing them.

## the result

Kids averaged 5.66 mentions per character. GPT-4 averaged 3.15, a pretty huge
gap (Cohen's d = 2.2). Then we ran the same book through six models, 30 stories
each, and the gap shrinks with every generation:

```
model                 gap vs kids (d)
gpt-4 (2024)          2.20
gpt-4 turbo           1.85
gpt-5.5               1.75
gpt-6.1 sol           0.94
claude haiku 5.5      0.93
claude opus 5.5       0.42   (not significant)
claude sonnet 5.5     0.33   (not significant)
```

[[demo:kids-gap]]

Opus and Sonnet tell this story with the same referential cohesion as a
four to six year old (none of the models go past the kids yet, though).

## kids and models get there differently

Matching on chain length doesn't mean the stories look alike. Kids lean on
pronouns, "it ... it ... he", sometimes for a character they never actually
introduced: they left about 0.87 pronouns per story that couldn't be tied to
anyone, vs 0.20 or fewer for every model. Models do the opposite, introducing
each character explicitly and then varying how they refer to it ("a fluffy
dog", "the pup"). So they land on similar cohesion through pretty
different strategies, and my guess is the kids are narrating their own picture of the scene, while the models write for a
reader.

## what's next

Seems to me chain length is a good first measure, and frontier models have
basically caught up on it. The next thing I'd want to look at is whether a
storyteller introduces a character before referring back to it, and whether
the story has real causal structure ("he knocked it over, so the cat ran"),
which is much closer to what we mean by a coherent story. Code and model
outputs are [on GitHub](https://github.com/mariopenglee/llm-child-narratives)
(the children's transcripts stay private).


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cyclediffusion.md -->
---
title: cyclediffusion: can a picture be a bottleneck?
date: 2026-10-17
summary: I trained a diffusion model so a captioner could read its pictures back into the original sentence. Instead of inventing a secret visual code, it collapsed into texture, and the reason is the reader you train against.
---

If you force a picture to carry a sentence, text to image and back to text,
does the picture stay something a person can read, or does it drift into a
private code only the captioner understands? I trained that loop, and it
didn't learn a code. Left alone it collapsed into carpet-like texture, and
the captioner happily described every image as "a man standing in front
of a wall that says 'The Wall'".

## the setup

The idea is an autoencoder whose bottleneck is a picture you can open and
look at, the same instinct as natural language autoencoders
([transformer-circuits, 2026](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/nla/))
but in pixels. It started as a project on relational representations in
visual models at UCLA's Computational Vision & Learning Lab, with Andrew Lee
and Hongjin Lu.

A caption goes into Stable Diffusion
([code](https://github.com/mariopenglee/cyclediffusion)), and a frozen
Pix2Struct captioner scores how likely the original caption is given the
generated image. That score is the cycle loss, and it trains the diffusion
UNet. For the gradient to reach the image I rewrote Pix2Struct's patch
extraction and flattening as pure tensor ops, so the whole loop is
differentiable. A second term, the usual denoising loss on real COCO
image-caption pairs weighted by lambda, ties the model to real pictures, and
lambda=0 is the pure cycle.

## what it learned

Each checkpoint generated images for 200 held-out COCO captions, scored by
the training critic (Pix2Struct), a captioner it never trained against
(BLIP), and CLIPScore:

```
change vs base              p2s_nll   blip_nll   clip
lambda=0, step 500            +0.14     +1.50    -13.0
lambda=1, step 750            -0.22     +0.18     -3.0
LoRA lambda=0.1, step 750     -0.11     +0.10     -1.5
```

With the pure cycle the images turn into carpet and stone-wall textures,
BLIP calls them "a close up of a carpet", and even the critic's own score
gets worse. With the anchor, the critic's score improves while BLIP and CLIP
get worse, so my read is the generator is learning to please one specific
reader rather than to carry the meaning.

[[demo:cycle-critic]]

## the reader is the bottleneck

My guess is the reason is the critic. This Pix2Struct checkpoint was fine-tuned on
TextCaps, captions about text inside images, and even on the untouched model's
pictures it describes a kitchen as "a building with a clock that says
10:00". Train against it and the generator inherits that fixation on signs
and shirts that say things.

So it seems to me a readable bottleneck is only as readable as the reader
you train it against. A narrow critic hands you its biases, and with nothing
anchoring the loop to real images it finds a degenerate picture rather than a
clever code. Next I'd like to swap in BLIP-large as the reader and see whether
a captioner that actually describes scenes keeps the pictures honest.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/phonetic5.md -->
---
title: A transformer that passes the wug test
date: 2026-10-16
summary: I fine-tuned T5 to turn spelling into IPA. Nobody told it English phonology rules, but it says "wugs" with a /z/ and "wuks" with an /s/, just like a kid does.
---

In 1958 Jean Berko Gleason showed children a made-up creature, said "this
is a wug", showed two of them and waited. The kids said "two wugs" with a
/z/ at the end, not an /s/, for a word they had never heard. There was
nothing to remember, so they must have learned a rule: the plural is voiced after a
voiced sound and devoiced after a voiceless one, so "bugs" ends in /z/ and
"bats" in /s/.

I wanted to know if a transformer that only ever sees spelling and
pronunciation learns that rule too, or basically just memorizes a dictionary.

## the setup

The task is grapheme to phoneme (G2P): text in, IPA out. Older G2P systems
are built from rules that linguists write by hand. I didn't give the model
any. I fine-tuned T5 small, base and large (60M to 770M parameters) on
about 113k English word and IPA pairs from ipa_dict, and added the IPA
symbols to the tokenizer so the model could actually write them. That's the
whole training signal: words and how they're pronounced, no phonology.

I also built two English to IPA sequence datasets for future work and put
them on Hugging Face
([ipa_dict_seq2seq](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mariopeng/openIPAseq2seq),
[OpenWebIPA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mariopeng/openwebIPA)).

## the wug test

Then I gave every model words that aren't in the data, built as minimal
pairs:

```
prompt    t5-small    t5-base     t5-large
wuks      [wəks]      [wəks]      [wəks]
wugs      [wəgz]      [wəgz]      [wəgz]
musips    [məsəps]    [mjuzɪps]   [mjuzɪps]
```

All three models pass. "wuks" and "wugs" differ only in whether the
consonant before the s is voiced, and the models flip the plural from /s/
to /z/ exactly where a native speaker does. The /z/ in "wugs" can't be
copied from the spelling (the spelling says s), so it seems to me the model
picked up the rule itself.

[[demo:wug-test]]

The same thing shows up on loan words. No model would write the /ts/
cluster at the start of "tsunami", because English words can't start that
way. The bigger the model, the closer it got to how a native speaker says
words like "coyote", "chow mein" and "receipt". My guess is scale buys
phonotactics (the rules for which sound sequences are allowed) pretty much the
same way it buys syntax.

## what it means

A speaker's sense of what sounds like English ("brick" yes, "bnick" no)
comes from the words they know, and a model trained on nothing but words
ends up with a piece of the same knowledge. That makes these models a
cheap way to test ideas about how people learn sound rules, and since you
can look inside them, I'd love to find where in the network the voicing rule
actually lives.

The paper was published in the *UCLA Undergraduate Science Journal*
(2023) as "Transformer Phonotactics via IPA G2P Finetuning"
([preprint](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1UBAq5x_5ZNalz5k98V0eq55oVT-PO4VP/view)),
and you can try the model in the [demo](https://phonetic5.streamlit.app/).


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/diverse-names.md -->
---
title: Why linguists keep writing about John and Mary
date: 2026-10-15
summary: In linguistics papers, 30% of male names are John and 31% of female names are Mary. A good list of names doesn't fix that, because people still pick from it. A random generator does.
---

Open a linguistics paper and look at the example sentences. "John thinks
Mary left." A survey of 927 papers in three major journals found that
30% of all male names were John and 31% of all female names were Mary.
Male arguments showed up twice as often as female ones, and they were the
ones doing things. Textbooks look the same, and they haven't changed much
since the 1990s.

To be honest, I don't think anyone chooses this. When an example needs a
name and you're at a whiteboard, you reach for the first one in your head,
and that one pretty much comes from the culture you grew up in.

## a list isn't enough

The obvious fix is a curated list of diverse names, and good ones already
exist. My intuition is that it doesn't go far enough, since picking from a
list is still picking, and over a semester the same unconscious pull comes
back (even with a balanced list and good intentions).

So with Maura O'Leary and Rainey Williams we built the
[Diverse Names Generator](https://diversenamesgenerator.com/), which takes
the choice away. You press generate, or swipe a card in the Android app,
and get a random name from a database linguists curate, so there's
basically no moment where the bias gets to act.

[[demo:name-draw]]

## making random usable

Random is only useful if instructors actually reach for it in class, so
every name comes with what you need at that moment:

- an IPA transcription, so you can say it confidently
- its usual gender association and the languages it comes from
- sometimes a recording, its native script, and famous people who share it

Filters keep the randomness compatible with the example. Semanticists need
one name per first letter so the initials don't collide in logic notation,
syntacticians need to match gender features, and one filter keeps to
English phonotactics for instructors worried about unfamiliar clusters.
Inside those constraints the pick is still random. The app downloads the
filtered set once with a single database call, then generates from that
local list, so it works offline in a classroom with bad wifi and never
shows the same name twice in a row.

The names come from users and students. Phonetics instructors can give
their students credit for submitting a name with a recording, which turns
an IPA exercise into something that ends up in front of other classes.
Linguists check every submission by hand before it goes into the pool.
When we published, the database had over 200 names from more than 30
languages.

## why the default matters

My view is that the bias here isn't really in anyone's values, it's in
which name comes to mind first, and that's pretty hard to train away.
Changing the default seems much easier than changing the person. I'd be
curious whether the same move works for other defaults in teaching
materials (example cities, job titles), probably interesting to check how
much the examples in a course actually shift once the generator is in use.

The paper is in the
[*Proceedings of the LSA*](https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/PLSA/article/view/5541)
(2023), and we presented it at the LSA 2023 Annual Meeting.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cross-seed-saes.md -->
---
title: Do sparse autoencoders capture manifolds?
date: 2026-07-15
summary: A concept like "year" lives on a curved manifold, and a single sparse autoencoder often shatters it instead of capturing it whole. Training several SAEs that differ only in random seed and pooling them tiles the manifold back together, right where one SAE dilutes it.
---

The representation of a year inside a language model isn't a point, it's a
helix: a periodic part (the decade digit) wound around a linear axis (the
century). Color traces a curved surface, days of the week trace a ring. A lot
of concepts are like this. They live on smooth low-dimensional manifolds
rather than single directions, which raises an awkward question for the main
tool we use to read models. A
[sparse autoencoder (SAE)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features)
is built to break an activation into a few discrete atoms, so what does it do
with a continuous curved surface?

Often it doesn't capture it cleanly. That's the finding in Bhalla et al.,
["Do Sparse Autoencoders Capture Concept Manifolds?" (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119):
instead of allocating a compact group of atoms that span the manifold (they
call this global capture), an SAE tends to shatter it into many atoms that
each tile a small local patch, or land in a fragmented in-between they call
dilution. My follow-up question was pretty simple. SAE training is stochastic, so each
random seed shatters the manifold a bit differently. If you train several SAEs
that differ only in seed and pool their atoms, do the different shatterings
tile the manifold more fully than any single one does?

The short answer from a [small POC](https://github.com/mariopenglee/cross-seed-manifold-poc)
is yes, and the benefit shows up where a single SAE gives up.

## where pooling helps

I used a synthetic benchmark from the paper (48 manifolds, circles and helices
and swiss rolls, placed in a 128-dim space), because the geometry is known and
reconstructions can be scored against ground truth. A manifold's fate is set by
the TopK sparsity `k`. Near `k` equal to the manifold's dimension a single SAE
captures it compactly from a handful of atoms, and pooling adds basically
nothing. As `k` grows the SAE dilutes the manifold across redundant atoms, and
that's where pooling pulls ahead: the gap in a few-atom reconstruction score
grows from about +0.01 at clean capture to roughly +0.1 at deep dilution, so
the benefit basically tracks dilution.

## the intuition, to play with

The demo below is a toy version of the mechanism (not a real SAE, just the
geometry). Pick a helix, sphere, or torus, the kind of shape a real concept
traces, and drag to spin it. Each seed scatters atoms over the manifold, and
each covers a small patch. The score is few-atom capture: how much the best
handful of patches tile, which is what the paper's metric rewards. One seed
leaves gaps, a second seed's gaps land elsewhere, so the pooled panel fills in
where the single-seed panel has holes (turn on "color by seed" to see which
seed covers what). Push the sparsity `k` up into dilution and the gap grows.

The third panel is the one I'd look at. It's one SAE as wide as the whole
pool (same total atoms and compute), and I'd have expected it to win, but at
high `k` it can fall behind even a single narrow seed. My guess at why: with
the same sparsity budget spread over more atoms, each one specializes to a
finer patch, and a few fine patches tile less of the manifold than a few
coarse ones.

[[demo:manifold-tiling]]

## tiling, not cleaner copies

The wide control rules out the obvious worry (that pooling just wins on atom
count) since it has those atoms and still loses. The other question was whether
the pool's gain is complementary coverage or just denoised copies of one
solution. I aligned each seed's atoms to a reference and averaged the matched
ones. Averaging can clean up a shared solution but can't invent an atom in a
region no seed covered, and it recovered basically none of the gain (often it
came out worse than a single seed). The pool's improvement also concentrated on
the points the best single seed reconstructed worst, which seems to me pretty
strong evidence the seeds cover complementary regions. If you decompose the
gain, roughly half is just having several independent SAEs to draw from and
half is genuine seed diversity.

## what I'd hold loosely

This is toy data with known geometry and one reconstruction metric, and it's a
few-percent effect, not a step change. I still think it's interesting
because seed variation usually gets filed as instability, and here it behaves
more like coverage (which you can pool).

The catch is that on a real model you can't score against ground truth, since
you don't know the manifold. So the test I actually care about is next, to pool
seeds on Llama-3.1-8B activations for concepts whose geometry we can at least
guess (years, colors, days), and see whether the places the seeds diverge are
where a single SAE was quietly diluting a concept. If pooled-seed agreement
can flag real manifold structure, it'd be a pretty cheap knob to have, so
would love to look into it.

(Update: the follow-up on Llama and Pythia is [here](#/blog/orphan-latents).)


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/block-grpo.md -->
---
title: block-GRPO: doing RL on a diffusion language model
date: 2026-05-09
summary: GRPO needs a log-probability that diffusion LLMs can't give you cheaply. Using the model's own block-autoregressive structure makes most of it exact, and it beat vanilla GRPO by about 10x on tail reward.
---

GRPO needs one number from your model: the log-probability of the sequence
it just generated. An autoregressive model hands it over for free. A
diffusion language model doesn't, and to be honest that gap is most of what
makes RL on one hard. My workaround was to lean on the model's own block
structure so most of that number becomes exact, and it beat vanilla GRPO by
about 10x on tail reward.

GRPO (group relative policy optimization, from DeepSeekMath, Shao et al.
2024) is the workhorse behind a lot of recent reasoning models. You sample a
group of completions, score them, and push the policy toward the
above-average ones, weighted by `log π(sequence)`. It basically assumes
that log-prob is exact and cheap. On a diffusion LLM it's neither, since
the model defines the sequence through an iterative denoising process, not a
left-to-right product of conditionals, so the exact likelihood is a sum over
denoising paths you can't enumerate.

## what diffu-GRPO did, and where it leaks

The prior work here is d1
([arxiv 2504.12216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12216)), whose diffu-GRPO
estimates the log-prob with a one-step approximation under random masking. It
works, but the estimate is biased in a way that compounds over training, so
you end up optimizing a noisy proxy (and the noise isn't mean-zero).

My angle was to stop fighting the model's structure and use it. The target
here, Fast-dLLM v2
([weights](https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Fast_dLLM_v2_7B)),
isn't pure diffusion: it's block-autoregressive. It generates a block at a
time, left to right across blocks, denoising within each block. Seems to me
that's pretty much the handle GRPO wants: the sequence log-prob is exact
across blocks (a real chain rule over the block order) and only needs
approximating inside each one, so the hard part shrinks from the whole
sequence to a single block.

[[demo:block-factorization]]

## three estimators for the within-block term

Within a block you still owe an intractable likelihood, so I tried three
ways to approximate it, trading bias for compute:

- **Masked (baseline):** the cheap one-step estimate, kept for comparison.
- **Per-block ELBO (default):** a proper evidence lower bound on the block
  likelihood, averaged over masking levels. More compute than masked, much
  less bias, and it's a bound rather than a point guess.
- **Gauss-Legendre quadrature:** treat the masking-level average as an
  integral and place the evaluation points by quadrature instead of
  sampling, which gets the same accuracy from fewer samples.

The ELBO is the one I'd reach for by default. It's the cleanest
bias-for-compute trade, and it degrades gracefully when you can't afford
many samples.

## the result

Block-GRPO with the ELBO estimator beat vanilla GRPO by about 10x on tail
reward over training (+0.158 vs +0.017). My view is the tail is the number
to watch, since that's where the hard prompts live, and it's also where a
biased log-prob hurts most: when only a few completions in a group score
well, the update leans almost entirely on their log-probs, so any error in
those gets amplified instead of averaged out.

## where this goes

What I keep coming back to is that all of this complexity exists to get a
usable gradient through an intractable likelihood. Evolution strategies
(Salimans et al. 2017,
[arxiv 1703.03864](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03864)) skip that entirely:
perturb the parameters, keep what scores better, never compute a log-prob at
all. For a model whose likelihood is this awkward, trading exact gradients
for black-box search might be the natural move rather than a fallback. Probably
worth running ES head-to-head against block-GRPO on the same reward, one
variable at a time, and seeing which actually wins. Would love to look into
it.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/infinite-context-agents-wip-london.md -->
---
title: Infinite context agents, at WIP London
date: 2026-04-18
summary: At WIP, an Index Ventures x Anthropic event for London AI builders, I presented memgit, git-backed memory that lets agents keep context across sessions instead of starting from zero.
---

![On stage at WIP: Index Ventures x Anthropic, London](/talk-anthropic-wip.jpg)

Agents forget everything between sessions, since the context window is the
only memory they have. In April I spent my slot at WIP, an event for
London's AI builders run by [Index Ventures](https://www.indexventures.com/)
and [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/), on how we were fixing that at
nexos.ai. The lineup had people from Anthropic, Revolut, Wiz, ElevenLabs,
incident.io and a few others, and the thing I presented was still
pre-launch, about a month into building, so it was also a good room to get
early feedback from.

The problem slide was pretty simple. Agents are stateless by default, so
every session starts from zero. Decisions and preferences get lost between
conversations, and multi-week work means re-explaining the project again and
again, so nothing an agent learns compounds.

memgit has the agent organize its own memory (rather than keeping a pile of
chat logs) and stores it in git. So memory has full history and can branch,
roll back and merge like code. Search runs over both keywords and vectors
(pgvector), and storage is tiered, with a capped hot set in Postgres. That's
what the "infinite" in the title means, to be honest: the history keeps
growing, while what the agent loads stays bounded. Each time the agent wakes
up (a heartbeat), it rebuilds its context from git as a stack:

[[demo:memgit-stack]]

This is close to the memory model I built for
[nexos.heartbeat](#/blog/heartbeat), the always-on AI twin, and that post
goes deeper on why memory should be a git repo. The git part is still the
bit I like most. It makes an agent's memory something you can diff and
audit, which seems to me pretty underrated for anything that runs
unsupervised. Deciding what an agent actually needs in front of it is also
pretty close to what I work on now at [condense.chat](https://condense.chat/),
just from the compression side.

People were skeptical, which was useful, and the pushback came down to two
things. The first was collaboration: what happens when several agents (or
people) write to the same memory at once? To be honest I think this is
where git shines, since concurrent edits are exactly what it was built for.
You just make sure every writer keeps pulling and always rebases, and race
conditions become ordinary merges.

The second, stale information, was the fair one. If memory only grows,
old facts sit next to new ones and the agent can't always tell which is
current. I don't have a full answer yet. My guess is that semantic sharding
(splitting memory by topic, so an update replaces the right slice instead
of piling up next to it) is probably the way to solve it.

Still, it held up in practice. All of nexos's company data ran through it,
and it worked fine. It would remember a meeting you'd had, start a draft
from it, and connect that to the right Jira ticket and the people involved,
all natively, just an agent with the right context. Most people at the
event seemed to come around to the same point: the hard part isn't storing
more, it's that we keep trying to fit everything into the context window.

The [LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7451194940912463872/)
has the full lineup.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/heartbeat.md -->
---
title: Building nexos.heartbeat: the infinite context problem
date: 2026-03-01
summary: An always-on AI twin doesn't have a context window problem, it has an infinite context problem. Information theory, the design space, and why our memory is a git repository.
---

An always-on assistant doesn't have a context window problem, it has an
infinite context problem, and to be honest that's a much deeper hole.

At nexos.ai my team has been building
[nexos.heartbeat](https://nexos.ai/heartbeat/), a digital AI twin: it
watches, learns, surfaces what matters, and acts before you ask.

## the infinite context problem

Context windows keep growing, so it's tempting to think the problem goes
away on its own. My view is it doesn't, since the input isn't a document, it's
a stream: every thread, meeting, draft, and half-decision, every day,
forever. No window holds an unbounded stream, and storage was never the hard
part (logs are cheap). The hard part is that at any moment almost none of the
past matters, and you don't know in advance which part does.

## memory is compression

Shannon's definition of information is surprise, and by that definition most
of the stream carries almost none: the signal is sparse. So the system has
to compress, and lossless doesn't save you, since a losslessly compressed
unbounded stream is still unbounded. Lossy compression forces a value
judgment. Rate-distortion theory says you can't even define it without
choosing what it costs to lose something, and that choice is the actual
product decision. The information bottleneck (Tishby, Pereira, Bialek, 1999)
frames it pretty well: squeeze the stream through a bottleneck that keeps only what
predicts a chosen variable, and let that variable set the cost instead of
hand-picking one. For a twin the variable is action, not reconstruction, so
the question isn't "can it replay the past", it's "would it act differently
without this". Memory becomes a compressed belief state, sufficient
statistics for action.

The part I find counterintuitive is that a good twin is defined mostly by
what it ignores, and "gets smarter every day" basically means it compresses
you better. Compression and prediction are the same quantity seen from two
sides, so acting before you ask is just prediction crossing a confidence
threshold.

## the design space

The naive version is hierarchical RAG: embed everything, retrieve top-k,
summarize, repeat up a tree. It works until the part that matters today is
something you compressed away yesterday, because it didn't look important at
the time (fixed summarization is lossy in a direction you chose too
early).

What I think you actually want is memory you can revise: keep the compressed belief
state, but let new evidence reopen old conclusions. So the structure isn't a
summary, it's a versioned model of the user that updates as you learn.

## memory as a git repository

The design I keep coming back to is a repository of structured plain-text
files, versioned like code. State lives in readable files (who the user is,
what they're working on, what they care about), and every update is a diff
against that state. The history of diffs is the timeline: not a log of
events, but a log of how the model of the user changed.

This gets you a few things pretty much for free. Many processes can
propose updates and you reconcile them like merges. A conflict between an
old assumption and new evidence becomes a merge conflict, which you resolve
explicitly instead of silently overwriting. You can read, in plain text,
why the twin believes what it believes, and roll back when it's wrong. And
branches let you hold tentative models of the user, only committing once
they're confirmed.

[[demo:belief-repo]]

We picked plain text because it's about as durable and merge-friendly as
formats get, and because a human (or another model) can read the state and
tell you it's wrong, which seems to me like the main thing a belief state
needs.

## where this goes

The open question I find most interesting is when to act. A twin that acts
on every high-confidence prediction gets exhausting pretty fast, and one
that waits for certainty is basically useless. My guess is the threshold
itself should be learned per person, from whether past actions landed, and
that feedback loop (act, see how it lands, update the threshold) is probably
the actual product, and I'd love to write more about it once we've pushed on it
further.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/code-interpreter-nexos.md -->
---
title: Code interpreter: how we built it ourselves
date: 2026-01-30
summary: How the nexos.ai code interpreter lets a model run real code instead of guessing: what it is for, and the isolated, ephemeral micro-VM sandbox behind it.
---

*Originally published by nexos.ai on LinkedIn, Jan 30, 2026 ([original](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/code-interpreter-how-weve-built-ourselves-nexos-ai-hgckf)). Mirrored here so it stays available.*

![Code interpreter: how we've built it from the ground up](/article-code-interpreter.png)

Code Interpreter improves your interaction with AI. This feature marks a fundamental shift from probability to precision. Standard LLMs predict and generate the next most likely word in a sentence, which can (and do) lead to hallucinations when handling complex arithmetic or logic. Our Code Interpreter solves this by allowing the model to write and execute actual code to derive answers.

Whether your teams need to calculate compound interest rates, solve complex logistics algorithms, or process precise date-time logic, the model generates executable scripts to produce exact results. This ensures that the numerical data and logic provided are not guesses, but computationally verified facts.

## Deep data analysis & insights

The Code Interpreter transforms the LLM into an expert data analyst capable of handling your organisation's most complex datasets. Users can simply upload raw files (such as a quarterly financial Excel spreadsheet or a CSV of customer logs) and instruct the model to perform rigorous quantitative tasks.

## Automated content & asset creation

Beyond analysis, this feature streamlines the actual production of business documents by generating files. It allows your teams to move from raw ideas to finalised documents without wasting time on manual formatting.

- Perform AI-powered research and make findings downloadable in a ready-made, formatted document:

- Generate agendas based on meeting notes, past comms, and other data in an easily-sharable format:

- Merge files and/or create multiple files based on the AI request:

- Create AI-generated reports in data, project progress, and more.

## A secure alternative for daily data tasks

Shadow IT – employees using unverified, third-party websites for file conversion or editing – poses a significant risk. The Code Interpreter eliminates this need by bringing these features in-house to a governed and fully observable AI platform.

Whether an employee needs to convert a sensitive PDF to a Word doc, resize a batch of high-resolution images, or edit a video clip, they can now do so within your sanctioned infrastructure. This provides a safe, internal mechanism for file manipulation, ensuring proprietary data never leaves your secure ecosystem to be processed by "free" online tools.

Building security and isolation

We understand that enabling code execution raises valid security questions, which is why we have built this feature with a defense-in-depth architecture.

All code generated by the LLM runs in a strictly isolated, ephemeral sandbox environment. This means the execution layer is completely firewalled from the internet. The environment is spun up solely for the duration of the user session and is immediately destroyed afterward. This allows your teams to leverage the power of executable code while maintaining strict compliance and data governance standards.

## How does Code Interpreter work behind the scenes

Every execution runs inside an isolated, ephemeral micro-VM with syscall filtering, filesystem whitelisting, and hard network egress blocks at the virtualization layer. This design ensures code cannot escape its environment or interact with external systems – giving teams the freedom to run complex logic without security exposure.

The file workflow balances safety with usability. Computation happens in a transient, sandboxed workspace, but any output files (spreadsheets, PDFs, slide decks) are promoted through a controlled persistence layer into your organisation’s secure storage. Users gain durable, shareable artifacts without exposing raw execution state or risking data leakage.

Each micro-VM is destroyed immediately after execution, while encrypted metadata-level audit logs provide compliance visibility without capturing customer data. The result is a system that delivers the flexibility of real code execution with enterprise-grade guarantees: hardened isolation, strict governance, and a seamless end-user experience.

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/rethinking-rag.md -->
---
title: RAG isn't dead, plain RAG is
date: 2025-12-04
summary: Why plain RAG breaks on real enterprise knowledge, and what organizing that knowledge first (late chunking, topic clusters, models that navigate a knowledge tree) changes. With Povilas Nagrockas.
---

*Originally published by nexos.ai on LinkedIn, Dec 4, 2025 ([original](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/rethinking-rag-why-knowledge-organization-new-competitive-advantage-kxkze)). Mirrored here so it stays available.*

![RAG isn't dead, plain RAG is, by Mario Peng Lee and Povilas Nagrockas](/article-rag.png)

*Published as "Rethinking RAG: why knowledge organization is the new competitive advantage", written with Povilas Nagrockas.*

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) began as a breakthrough, but in practice it has become a default pattern that rarely meets modern needs. Most teams implement it expecting it to “just work,” only to run into brittle pipelines, inconsistent answers, and retrieval systems that fall apart when confronted with real enterprise complexity.

And today’s complexity is very different from the early days of RAG.

Finding a single relevant passage – the classic needle-in-a-haystack task –  is no longer the real challenge. In the agentic era, models must retrieve and reason over multi-step, cross-document, cross-topic context, often spanning dozens of sources and evolving over time. That level of integrated understanding is simply out of reach for naive RAG systems.

Our past year inside large, sensitive, constantly shifting enterprise data environments made something uncomfortably clear:

Plain, naïve RAG is obsolete - because retrieval without organization is chaos.

Enterprises don’t struggle with retrieval because their vectors are bad. They struggle because the knowledge feeding these vectors is fragmented, unsanitized, and mis-chunked. Good retrieval cannot emerge from disordered information.

To better understand how to build better RAG, we need to look at the components that make up RAG. One of the most important ones is knowledge organization, so by tackling how the knowledge is stored, we essentially facilitate how it's retrieved, both for humans and LLMs to have a clear trace and understanding of it.

## The Real Bottleneck: Unstructured Knowledge

Across clients we repeatedly saw the same patterns:

- Documents split into arbitrary pieces with context shattered across chunk boundaries.

- Semantically similar chunks producing ambiguous or misleading retrieval.

- Vector spaces lacking hierarchy, relationships, and structure.

RAG pipelines were doing exactly what they were told to do - but on top of disorganized data. So we turned our focus to the Knowledge Organization.

## Knowledge organization: the foundation RAG never had

High-quality retrieval starts with structure, not with bigger embeddings or longer context windows. Our approach builds this foundation by transforming messy data into navigable knowledge:

- Context-aware chunking that respects semantic boundaries

- Clustering and topic hierarchies that reorganize content into meaningful layers

- Entity- and feature-extraction that adds metadata richness

- Relationship modeling that sets the stage for graph-based reasoning

The result is not “better RAG” - it’s integrated knowledge, something closer to how humans learn and traverse information.

Instead of acting like a system that occasionally looks up answers in a recipe book, the model behaves as if it has learned the recipes. It doesn’t just retrieve a passage; it understands how the pieces fit together, and can use that understanding to reason through novel, unseen problems. From a technical perspective, the effect is similar to what you’d get if the model were fine-tuned on the entire corpus:

the knowledge becomes structurally embedded into the model’s reasoning process, producing context-aware, cross-document insights that simple retrieval pipelines cannot achieve.

This shift (from lookup to understanding, from fragments to integration) is the foundation RAG has always lacked.

## Late chunking: document-aware embeddings without the heavy hand of LLMs

We employed a novel technique called Late chunking:

- We embed the document at the token level, producing highly granular vectors that already carry whole-document semantic awareness. As the document is processed, we maintain a running semantic summary that enriches each token’s embedding with global context.

- After embedding do we split and pool (average) these token-level vectors into chunks, ensuring that every resulting chunk embedding remains whole-document aware rather than isolated to a narrow window.

This yields context-rich chunk vectors without resorting to LLM-heavy preprocessing, avoiding both hallucination risks and the compute costs associated with LLM-driven chunking approaches.

## Building topic clusters: from chaos to structure

Once chunk embeddings exist, we cluster them to build a hierarchical “knowledge tree.” Think of it as document-aware vectors, nested topics and subtopics, and a graph-like structure the model can navigate.

By adding optional LLM-generated cluster summaries, the structure becomes self-describing and easy for users to interpret. And this foundation enables something far beyond retrieval: guided traversal of knowledge, where the system can surface not just answers but relevant directions, themes, and next steps.

We’re already building on this capability inside [nexos.ai](http://nexos.ai) - upcoming Projects features like conversation starters and conversation continuations will leverage this structured understanding to help users explore their data more intelligently and proactively.

## Models that navigate the knowledge tree

Instead of relying solely on cosine similarity or pooled vectors, we let the model reason through structure:

- A query-extractor rewrites the user’s question into targeted, keyword-dense prompts.

- The model traverses the cluster graph - moving up, down, or across topics.

- It identifies the most relevant nodes before performing final retrieval.

This hybrid agentic + structural approach already shows measurable gains:

+9% accuracy over DPR and +10% over BM25. But it’s important to note that these benchmarks reflect mostly needle-in-a-haystack tasks. The real challenge – multi-document, cross-topic reasoning –  is much harder to quantify, and simple RAG systems consistently fail at it.

In practice, our system delivers substantial qualitative improvements on these complex queries, where structured traversal and context-anchored reasoning matter far more than raw similarity scores.

Of course, this added reasoning introduces some latency and increased token usage. Like any technical choice, it’s a tradeoff - one that should be evaluated against the complexity, stakes, and performance needs of each specific use case.

## What this means for enterprises?

Enterprises benefit from retrieval that is not only relevant but deeply context-anchored, supported by transparent and traceable reasoning, reduced dependence on fragile prompt engineering, and a system resilient enough to handle dynamic, sensitive, high-volume data - ultimately creating an environment where LLM-based agents can act rather than merely answer.

And this is only the beginning: we are advancing toward drift-resilient structures that adapt to constantly changing data, integrating methods like BM-25, SBERT, and grammar-based chunking for code, and developing richer graph-based reasoning through agentic traversal, all with a single goal - equipping models not just with information, but with the structural intelligence required to truly think.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/context-engineering.md -->
---
title: Context engineering: where AI stops guessing
date: 2025-11-19
summary: The hard part of enterprise AI isn't a bigger model, it's getting the right documents, rules and situational awareness in front of the model before it answers.
---

*Originally posted on LinkedIn, Nov 19, 2025 ([original](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mariopenglee_the-real-challenge-in-enterprise-ai-today-share-7396873975009751040-niZ9/)). Mirrored here so it stays available.*

![Context engineering: where AI stops guessing](/article-context-engineering.jpg)

The real challenge in enterprise AI today isn’t chasing ever-larger models, it’s giving those models the context they need to make decisions that actually reflect your business.

Organizations that excel at context engineering are already capturing far more value from their AI investments.

## what is context engineering

When an AI model generates an answer, it relies on the context it receives in the moment, NOT generic training data.
Context engineering is systematically designing how information flows into your AI systems. It ensures your models respond with your business reality in mind: your policies, data, and processes.

In other words: context replaces generic output with grounded, business-aware reasoning.

## why this matters now

Most enterprises deploy LLMs for support, knowledge search, or workflow assistance, but quickly hit a barrier: the model isn't grounded in your business reality.

Context engineering bridges that gap. It's the architectural layer ensuring every AI response pulls from:
- The right documents
- The right rules
- The right situational awareness

Imagine an employee asks your internal AI: "Can I offer a 15% discount to this customer?"

A well-designed context layer automatically surfaces current pricing policies, contract terms, and required approvals, before the model even begins generating an answer.

That's context-aware decision support that's consistent, compliant, and scalable across your organization.

## the impact

- Higher productivity -> less time wasted on repetitive searches
- Reduced risk -> consistent adherence to policies
- Faster scaling -> AI assistants that adapt as your data grows

When AI truly understands your business context, your teams actually trust its answers.
